source.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Binary and Ternary Transformers

record.tranche_reason: Applies grokking measurements to binary and ternary transformers on modular addition, extending the finding to a new model setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports grokking outcomes and mechanistic findings for its own binary and ternary models. It also reports Fourier-structure comparisons relevant to algorithm similarity. Figure-only details are not included where the text provides no explicit outcome.
record.test_reason: It trains binary and ternary one-layer transformers on modular addition (P=113) and reports whether they grok, with and without weight decay. It also compares their Fourier structure with full-precision models. This is the original algorithmic setting with a new kind of network.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Binary and ternary transformers show grokking similar to full precision (with weight decay) and learn similar Fourier-based algorithms. These are not more interpretable and seem less so because of noise. This is evidence against using such networks as a more interpretable alternative. The exact algorithm learned is not conclusively identified.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular addition and a one-layer transformer setup related to the cited grokking work, but binarizes or ternarizes most linear layers and uses a straight-through estimator; it adds RMSNorm before the unembedding. The embedding and unembedding layers are not binarized or ternarized.
record.method_sensitivity: Grokking is reported with weight decay and absent without it; binary models are described as grokking in fewer epochs and overfitting less initially than full-precision results.
record.problems: The reported grokking curves use loss rather than accuracy, and the paper gives no training-set-size sweep. Only modular addition is studied. The authors say they lack conclusive evidence about the exact learned algorithm; the binary analysis has added noise, and the paper notes that multiple algorithms may solve the task.

untested.parts: Test accuracy jumping from chance to near-perfect (only loss is shown); the size of the delay; dependence of the delay on training-set size.
Entire version: no time-resolved circuit formation or progress measures.
Entire version: no non-algorithmic data and no initialization-scale or norm sweep.
Efficiency mechanism, critical dataset size, ungrokking. Only the presence or absence of weight decay is varied.
Variation across seeds, runs and hyperparameters; conclusive identification of the algorithm.
Entire version: no optimizer or floating-point controls.

missing.what: Binary networks grok in much fewer epochs and overfit less early than full precision. This bears on the size of the delay under constrained weights.
Degree-2 single-frequency polynomials explain neuron variance clearly less well in the binary model than in full precision; ternary is in between.

record.verdict_notes: Short single-author preprint with no quantitative grokking timing and no seeds or error bars. Weight decay was described as necessary, so the r3/r4 finding rests on a single sentence. Weight decay matters to V5, but the study does not test the efficiency account, so r3/r4 are linked to V1 only.

versions.untested_parts: Uses loss rather than accuracy, and does not compare training-set sizes or quantify how the delay changes as the dataset shrinks.
No time-resolved measurements of circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, or continuous progress measures anticipating the generalization jump.
No non-algorithmic datasets or initialization-scale/weight-norm transition sweep.
No realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Although it compares training with and without weight decay, it does not test the proposed efficiency mechanism, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
Compares binary and ternary models with full-precision results, but does not test variation across multiple runs, seeds, architectures, or hyperparameter settings.
No adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point softmax artifact controls.

rows.subject: binary transformer
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with weight decay
rows.measure: Training and test loss trajectory / grokking
rows.value: The paper reports grokking; train loss converges to around 0.006 and test loss to around 0.01.
rows.note: The paper says binary networks grok under weight decay. It does not give accuracy values or quantify the delay in text.
rows.check: Grokking is stated in the text and shown in the Figure 1 loss curve. The value given (converged losses 0.006/0.01) is end-state loss, not the delay. No accuracy and no delay length appear in the text.

rows.subject: ternary transformer
rows.stage_stated: trained; epoch count not stated for this result
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with weight decay
rows.measure: Training and test loss trajectory / grokking
rows.value: The paper reports grokking; train and test loss converge to around 0.03 for both.
rows.note: The text says ternary models exhibit grokking. No accuracy values or delay duration are given.
rows.check: Same as r1. Figure 4 appears to show about 10k epochs, but the epoch count is not stated for the ternary run. The 0.03 converged loss is end-state, not delay evidence.

rows.subject: binary transformer
rows.baseline: With weight decay, binary networks consistently exhibit grokking.
rows.value: The paper states that binary networks do not exhibit grokking without weight decay.
rows.note: Explicit no-weight-decay comparison; no corresponding numerical curve value is stated.
rows.check: The baseline is the study's own weight-decay run. The match to full precision 'as found in Nanda' is a cited comparison, not a result of this study. No curves or numbers are shown for the no-weight-decay runs.

rows.subject: ternary transformer
rows.baseline: With weight decay, ternary networks consistently exhibit grokking.
rows.value: The paper states that ternary networks do not exhibit grokking without weight decay.
rows.note: Explicit no-weight-decay comparison; no corresponding numerical curve value is stated.
rows.check: Same as r3. The finding is a single shared sentence in §4.1 with no figure.

rows.subject: binary transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared Fourier structure and algorithmic features with full-precision modular-addition results
rows.measure: Similarity of learned algorithm, assessed through embedding/logit Fourier structure
rows.baseline: Full-precision results described in the cited modular-addition work.
rows.value: The paper reports periodicity in embeddings and logits like the full-precision model, and characterizes the learned algorithms as similar and Fourier-transformation-based.
rows.note: The paper also reports significant noise in the binary model's Fourier-basis projections and says it lacks conclusive evidence about the exact algorithm learned.
rows.check: The comparison crosses architectures (binary vs full precision), not seeds or runs. The full-precision comparison partly relies on Nanda et al. Figure 5 shows a lower degree-2 FVE for binary neurons, which is a real difference the value omits.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V6. Binary models show similar embedding/logit periodicity and noisier Fourier projections, but the exact learned algorithm is not conclusively identified.
source_check.problem: Fourier similarity and poorer fits do not establish whether models converge to the same or different algorithms.

rows.subject: ternary transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared Fourier structure and algorithmic features with full-precision modular-addition results
rows.measure: Similarity of learned algorithm, assessed through embedding/logit Fourier structure
rows.baseline: Full-precision results described in the cited modular-addition work.
rows.value: The paper reports the same periodicity as the binary and full-precision models; ternary results fall between binary and full precision and are closer to full precision in noise level.
rows.note: The paper cautions that it cannot conclusively identify the exact algorithm learned and notes that different algorithms may be learned for modular addition.
rows.check: No problem with the row. The authors state the exact algorithm cannot be identified (clock vs pizza).

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V6. Ternary models retain periodicity and have less noise than binary models; the exact learned algorithm remains unidentified.
source_check.problem: Intermediate noise and Fourier-fit quality do not demonstrate incomplete algorithm convergence or a different algorithm.
